title: Diversification and position sizing

overview.objective: Keep any single trade, or any group of linked trades, from doing serious damage.
overview.holdingPeriod: Applies to every trade, whatever its length.
overview.context: A risk principle for all markets and strategies. It does not make any strategy profitable; it limits damage.

simple.simple: Decide how much you can lose on one trade before you enter, and size the trade from your [[stop-loss]] so you cannot lose more. Treat trades that depend on the same thing as one bigger bet.
simple.balanced: [[position-sizing|Position sizing]] turns a fixed [[risk-per-trade]] into a trade size: risk in money ÷ (stop distance × value per point). [[diversification|Diversification]] only helps when positions do not move together, and [[correlation|correlations]] tend to rise in stressed markets. Gaps can still push a loss past the stop.

reasoning: Every strategy has losing streaks. Keeping each loss small, and not stacking linked losses, could keep an account usable through a streak long enough to see whether the strategy works. That is the reasoning; it limits damage but cannot turn losing rules into winning ones.

rules.label: A simplified educational version, not anyone's documented method
rules: Risk no more than 1% of the account on any single trade.
Size each trade from the stop: risk in money ÷ stop distance = value per pip or point.
Keep total open risk at no more than 5% of the account.
Treat trades that depend on the same currency, sector or commodity as one position, and keep their combined risk at no more than 2%.
Set the size before entering, and never widen a stop to keep a losing trade open.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under these rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A simulated 10,000 USD account with four open trades, each risking 1%: long EUR/USD, long GBP/USD, short USD/CHF and short USD/JPY.

options.explanation: Right: 4 × 1% = 4%. That is within the 5% total, but as one dollar bet it breaks the 2% limit for linked trades.

options.text: Each of the four tends to gain if the US dollar weakens broadly
options.explanation: Right: each trade is a bet against the dollar, so they are closely linked.

options.text: A fifth 1% trade, short USD/CAD, would spread the risk
options.explanation: No: it is another bet against the dollar, adding to the same exposure.

options.text: A 1% trade must not lose more than 100 USD at the stop
options.explanation: Right: 1% of 10,000 USD = 100 USD, so the size is set from the stop to keep the loss within that.

options.text: A sharp dollar rally would hit only the EUR/USD and GBP/USD trades
options.explanation: No: all four lose when the dollar rises, about 4% together, and more if prices gap past the stops.

failureAnalysis: Linked positions all lose together and the total loss is several times the per-trade limit.
Gaps jump past stops, so losses exceed the plan.
Moving stops further away to avoid a loss breaks the sizing.
Raising risk after a few wins makes the next streak more damaging.
limitations: The 1%, 2% and 5% figures are examples for learning, not recommendations for your situation.
Sizing limits losses; it does not make a strategy profitable.
Correlations change, and in stressed markets they often rise.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Account 8,000 USD, 1% risk, stop 40 pips. 1 pip is worth 1 USD per 10,000 units. What size?

options.explanation: No: that is the account size, not the trade size.
No: at 4 USD per pip, a 40-pip stop risks 160 USD, which is 2%.

options.text: 20,000 units: 80 USD ÷ 40 pips = 2 USD per pip
options.explanation: Right: 2 USD per pip is 20,000 units.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Three open trades are all long other currencies against the US dollar, at 1% risk each. What is the combined exposure most like?

options.explanation: Right: they all depend on the dollar falling.

options.text: Three separate 1% risks that cancel each other out
options.explanation: No: they move together; they do not cancel.

options.text: Less than 1% in total, because the currencies are spread across different regions
options.explanation: No: they share the same dollar exposure.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why risk a small fixed share of the account on each trade?

options.explanation: No: size does not change how often a trade wins.

options.text: A losing streak then leaves the account usable
options.explanation: Right: ten 1% losses leave about 90% of the account.

options.text: Because brokers require each trade to stay below a set share of the account
options.explanation: No: brokers set margin rules, but that is not why you size small.
